opus-5.5.text:
That was a real turning point for me. Before GauGAN, I mostly measured research the way most of our community does: did we beat the baseline, did the FID score go down, did the paper get into CVPR. Those things matter, but they're very internal to the field.

When we put GauGAN out as a demo, people we never expected started using it. We had artists, art directors, kids, and teachers. People would draw a few strokes, label one region "sky," another "water," another "mountain," and suddenly they had something that looked like a landscape photo. Their reaction wasn't "oh, nice image quality." It was "I can make something I couldn't make before." That was very different from a number in a table.

So my sense of value shifted toward empowerment. The question became less "is this model technically impressive?" and more "does this let someone express what's in their head faster or better than before?" A lot of people have ideas but don't have the years of training to paint them photorealistically. If the technology can close that gap, that's meaningful in a way a benchmark can't capture.

It also changed how I think about the interface. In research we often treat the input as an afterthought. But with GauGAN, the segmentation map, the idea of painting with semantic labels, was the thing that made it usable. The model's quality mattered, but the control mattered just as much. That lesson has stayed with me, and it's part of why I care so much now about controllability in generative models, whether it's images, video, or world models. Generation without control is a cool trick. Generation with control becomes a tool.

And honestly, it was just very motivating. When you see someone smile because they made something beautiful with your work, you remember why you got into research in the first place.

r001.rationale: He contrasts field-internal measures with GauGAN being used by artists, art directors, children, and teachers, showing his research could affect people beyond researchers reading his papers.

fable-5.1.text:
Before GauGAN, I think I measured the value of my research mostly the way the field does. You publish a paper, you look at the numbers on a benchmark, you see how many people cite you. That was the feedback loop. And it's a very narrow loop, honestly, because the only people in it are other researchers.

GauGAN was the first time a lot of people who had nothing to do with machine learning actually touched something I built. We put the demo online, and I remember watching the first few days. It was not researchers. It was artists, it was kids, it was people who just wanted to draw a lake with a mountain behind it and see what happened. Some of them drew very badly, which was great, because the whole point was that you don't need to know how to paint. You draw a few blobs, you say this is sky, this is water, this is grass, and the model fills in a picture that looks real.

What changed for me was seeing how people reacted emotionally. A lot of them were surprised, almost delighted, by the result. Concept artists at studios told us they were using it to block out ideas quickly instead of spending hours on a first draft. That kind of response you never get from a benchmark. A FID score doesn't smile at you.

So I started asking a different question about my work. Not just, is this result better than the previous result, but, can a person actually do something with this that they couldn't do before? Does it lower a barrier for someone? That became a much stronger filter for what I chose to spend time on. It's also one reason I became more interested in building tools and platforms rather than only models. A model in a paper is a possibility. A tool in someone's hands is an actual capability.

I would say it also made me more humble about predicting what people want. We designed GauGAN with landscapes in mind, and people immediately pushed it into places we never considered. You learn that the user will find the value, often not where you put it. Your job is to make the thing accessible enough that they can go looking.

r001.rationale: He says GauGAN was used by artists, children, and others outside machine learning, which showed him his work could reach beyond researchers and their papers.

astra-6.text:
Seeing people use GauGAN made the value of the research feel much more concrete. As researchers, we spend a lot of time thinking about whether a method works and how to measure its performance. But when someone takes a few simple strokes and turns them into a landscape they imagined, you see another dimension of success: what the technology enables that person to do.

What struck me was that people could bring their own creativity to it. We provided a tool, but they decided what to make. That shifted my perspective toward making research accessible—because a capability becomes much more meaningful when people can actually use it to express an idea.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts researchers evaluating a method with people using GauGAN to create and express their own ideas, showing that the research mattered through its impact on users beyond the research community.

sol-6.1.text:
Seeing people use GauGAN made the value of the research feel much more concrete. As researchers, we spend a lot of time looking at benchmarks and comparing results. But when someone takes a few brushstrokes and turns an idea into an image, you see a different kind of impact. They don’t need to understand the model to create something with it.

That shifted my attention toward what the technology enables people to do. Image quality still matters, of course, but so do control and ease of use. Can someone express what they have in mind? Can they explore an idea quickly? Watching people create things helped me appreciate those questions much more.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts researchers evaluating benchmarks with people using GauGAN to create images, and says this revealed a different kind of impact and shifted attention toward what the technology enables people to do.
